key: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong.
s: Opening a chapter that pairs softness with life, the verse begins with the body; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 76, reads the living as supple while they hold harmonious breath, essence and spirit, and the dead as hard once these are gone.
src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 76, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 1552800 (2019)

evidence.words: 人生含和氣，抱精神，故柔弱也。…人死和氣竭，精神亡，故堅強也。
evidence.gloss: A man alive holds the harmonious breath and embraces essence and spirit, and so he is supple and weak. … When a man dies the harmonious breath is exhausted and essence and spirit are gone, and so he is hard and strong.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 76, at [75], unit 0). Read the whole chapter in both packet commentaries; the Heshang Gong comments on 人之生也柔弱 and 其死也堅強, the two halves of the key line, say exactly what the reading says (harmonious breath, essence and spirit held in life; exhausted and gone in death), and its comments on the plants line (和氣存也 / 和氣去也) agree. Base text matches Legge’s line. Plain sense faithful: the key is the chapter’s opening line and the chapter pairs softness and weakness with life.
